First confirm that the file you have open is `src/Laravel/public/swagger-ui-bundle.js`, then read down through the file itself. What belongs here is not a dependency inventory, but the few references actually involved in value flow before the exit point. Walkthrough notes should distinguish references that only load the bundle from those that affect failure information or event data. For the former, you can note just the location; for the latter, continue to where they are read or rewritten.

## From state to exit points

The walkthrough on this page usually stops near the event exit point. During review, mark three things in the order they appear in the code:

- The last value retrieval or assignment before output;
- The statement where the event or failure information leaves the file;
- The conditional branch immediately adjacent to that statement.

Keeping these three together makes it easier to distinguish "a value was prepared in the file" from "that value actually reached the exit point." If a branch only changes a local variable without reaching the output, it must not be recorded as event behavior. Conversely, cleanup code after the output statement shouldn't be read back into the data carried by the event.

The previous version grouped "failure or event output locations" into a single walkthrough stop. That wording is retained to make navigation easier, but the two should be reviewed separately. A failure path may only hand off control flow elsewhere, and an event path may only pass out an object that has already been prepared. The available material doesn't establish a definitive event name, error text, or parameter shape, so no conclusions about these have been added.

## Margin notes for review

Whenever you encounter a possible exit point in the file, you can use short tags to capture the context without copying the entire bundle:

`[Read]` records which section of local code the value comes from; `[Condition]` records what the branch is testing; `[Output]` records whether the statement is an event output, failure handling, or still unclassified; `[Follow-up]` continues tracing only if a direct use is still visible in the same file.

Don't start by interpreting long variable names in business terms; the original names and locations are easier to check next time than guesses.

3. Before leaving the file, has the failure branch already changed the value that will be output?

Follow-up notes should go directly beside the corresponding exit point: adding the actual statement and the state changes just before it is enough. Without new observations from within the file, don't expand "possible receivers" into call relationships any further.

Local value retrieval or assignment

# ApiPlatform Call Relationships: Code Walkthrough

This page still starts at `src/OpenApi/Factory/OpenApiFactory.php`. It has repeatedly served as an entry point for reading code related to OpenAPI, for a simple reason: the schema factory interface, resource metadata, and collection operation types all appear at the top of the file. The early notes read too much into this convenience, though. The old wording was: "This file connects resources, collection operations, and schema into a single call chain." use ApiPlatform\JsonSchema\Schema;
use ApiPlatform\JsonSchema\SchemaFactoryInterface;
use ApiPlatform\Metadata\ApiResource;
use ApiPlatform\Metadata\CollectionOperationInterface;
```

Start with the upper group. `Schema` is a concrete type name, and `SchemaFactoryInterface` is a factory interface name. Seeing both at the top of the same file is enough to place the code-reading entry point on the JsonSchema side. The old page loosely called them the "schema side." That shorthand still works for navigation, but `Schema` and the factory interface should no longer be described as the same object. For changes where schema-related behavior needs checking, first establish whether the issue concerns this concrete type or the interface. Having the names next to each other does not mean the code that follows necessarily leads to the same place.

The lower group is the metadata side. `ApiResource` points to the resource object, and `CollectionOperationInterface` points to the collection operation interface. They sit in the same reading branch because both appear among the visible dependencies of `OpenApiFactory.php`, not because this page has already confirmed every combination of resources and collection operations. The "resources and collection operations" category in the old notes can stay: when tracing back from questions about resource configuration or collection endpoints, these two names are more useful stopping points than the filename.

The top of the file is therefore useful for pointing to two paths to trace back through, not for laying out a left-to-right flow:

```text
src/OpenApi/Factory/OpenApiFactory.php
│
├─ JsonSchema
│  ├─ Schema
│  └─ SchemaFactoryInterface
│
└─ Metadata
   ├─ ApiResource

To go on to assess the output shape, you should still choose the schema group first, rather than letting the presence of `ApiResource` settle the question.

# ApiPlatform callback relationships: code-reading notes

This page originally approached `src/GraphQl/Type/FieldsBuilder.php` on the assumption that "callbacks are produced centrally by a factory." That reading path has been retained because people still come here to look up names related to the GraphQL field; but it turned adjacency in the file header into an execution relationship and is no longer a suitable basis for drawing conclusions about the implementation.

## The original interpretation, preserved in substance

The first version arranged four imports into a neat sequence: the type definitions first gave fields their shape, the filter added filterable fields, and the parser factory then supplied callbacks; an unsuitable type caused an exit through an exception. On that reading, `FieldsBuilder.php` looked like the place every field callback had to pass through.

This conclusion was appealing because the names fit so well. The file path was under `GraphQl/Type`, and `ResolverFactoryInterface` sat right next to `TypeInterface`, so "field types" and "parser callbacks" were naturally linked into a single chain. But this was a working hypothesis made while reading the file header, not a relationship established from method calls, argument passing, or return values.

Two margin notes from that time are also retained:

- `FilterInterface` was treated as an optional input to field callbacks;
- `InvalidTypeException` was treated as the failure exit on this construction path.

These two notes explain why the first version also drew the filter and exception into the callback relationship. They provided no field names, call order, or conditions for raising an exception; the first version overlooked those gaps.

## What the file header actually confirms: adjacency

This review only rechecked the direct dependencies visible in this file, with the following results:

```php
use ApiPlatform\GraphQl\Exception\InvalidTypeException;
use ApiPlatform\GraphQl\Resolver\Factory\ResolverFactoryInterface;
use ApiPlatform\GraphQl\Type\Definition\TypeInterface;
use ApiPlatform\Metadata\FilterInterface;
```

These show that, at the namespace level, this file references GraphQL's type definitions, parser factory, filter metadata, and type exceptions. That is enough to provide a starting point for browsing the code: when investigating a field construction issue, you can first check whether the type definitions and parser factory are in the same context; when looking at filter-related field descriptions, there is no need to start a completely unrelated reading path.

But imports alone do not say which object creates another, whether `FilterInterface` is involved in a particular field, or who throws `InvalidTypeException`. The first version's mistake was equating "visible in the same file" with "must be called."

## The later correction did not establish a new conclusion

Following the review, the original claim that "`ResolverFactoryInterface` is the sole source of callbacks" should be treated as the old interpretation. The file header only supports treating it as one of the adjacent objects that need further investigation. Nor can `TypeInterface` be assumed to be a callback result type based on its name alone; it is simply a type-definition dependency this file directly declares it uses. The same applies to `FilterInterface` and `InvalidTypeException`.

This is not a matter of replacing the first version's arrows with a different set. The existing record provides no call snippets from this file, nor any interface implementation or caller, so this page should not add a seemingly complete execution sequence. The earlier diagram-based interpretation should stop here:

```text
FieldsBuilder.php
  ├─ TypeInterface
  ├─ ResolverFactoryInterface
  ├─ FilterInterface
  └─ InvalidTypeException
```

The diagram above only shows a sequence of direct dependency names to inspect while reading the code, not runtime flow. The first version's "type → filter → factory → callback" sequence can still help explain why this page was created, but can no longer be used to locate problems.

## Where to look when revisiting the code

If the issue concerns field types, start with the actual uses of `TypeInterface` in this file; if it points to parser callbacks, continue through the uses of `ResolverFactoryInterface`. The filter and exception should not be included up front unless they actually appear in the same section of code.

DOC-08 contains scattered notes on adjacent calls. It can help confirm which name to open next, but should not be used to retroactively fill in a nonexistent callback chain for this page. The two pages' earliest shared misreading was to treat adjacent imports as already verified call relationships.

This old code-reading record has not been removed: it preserves a very common initial misreading. When you come across this page later, you should first treat "callbacks are produced centrally by a factory" as a historical claim, then reconstruct the relationships from actual uses in the file.

# Parameter Shape History

When this page was first written, the objects discussed side by side in the parameter chain were scalar, collection, and existing array schema. At the time, they were all grouped under the broad term "parameter conversion," making them sound like three kinds of input to the same operation; the first real sticking point was whether the outer structure of public parameters that already had an array schema should be reworked in response to the new discussion of collection.

The initial choice recorded here was conservative. An existing array schema was not to be used as input for regenerating a collection representation. An explicitly specified scalar would keep its own schema for the time being; whether collection needed a different kind of public parameter would be decided once the item details were clearer.

Another option was to convert every parameter to an array. This would leave only one outer structure to deal with downstream, making it easier to explain. But it conflated "the input is already an array" with "forming a collection from an item." There is no reason at this point to consider the two interchangeable, so that option was not adopted.

This initial draft does not settle parameter names. `key` and any `key[]` that might appear are just markers for further review; on their own, they aren't enough to indicate whether the input comes from scalar or collection. form, deepObject, and explode have not yet been tied to the same parameter object either, so they cannot yet be documented as a stable pairing.

# Parameter shape history

## What still holds from the original trade-off

This page was not originally meant to provide a comprehensive table of OpenAPI parameters. It was meant to preserve a choice that was not resolved immediately: whether existing array schemas should be regenerated along with newly introduced collections. The first draft grouped scalar, collection, and array schema under "parameter conversion"; a later reread started by breaking up that grouping.

There were still only two options at the time.

- Leave existing schemas in place; consider explicit scalars and collection items separately, then decide whether a new parameter representation is needed.
- Normalize all inputs to arrays early, so downstream processing only has one outer shape to handle.

The second option had an obvious advantage: less text and fewer branches. That was also where the problem lay. If a schema that was already an array was expanded again as a collection, someone reading the result could not tell whether it was a collection representation for new input or a rearranged representation of an existing object. This page therefore retains the first option as the tentative decision; normalizing to arrays remains an earlier candidate, not a description of behavior.

## Three cases the review shifted its focus to

The fall review did not produce a complete output. It only shifted the focus to three questions: whether the input explicitly provided a scalar schema; whether a non-array item schema appeared on the collection path; and whether the input itself already carried an array schema.

These three questions all concern parameters, but they are distinct checks. For an explicit scalar, the focus is whether single-value semantics can be preserved. Only with a non-array item is there room to discuss a collection representation. An existing array schema must first be treated as an object to preserve; the presence of the first two input types must not send it down the "create a collection from an item" branch.

This wording is not meant to turn the three input types into a fixed workflow. It is meant to keep the old normalization wording from once again reducing the third type to a variant of the second. An existing array schema carries legacy compatibility implications; it is not an unfinished collection description.

`key` was kept as a separate item in the record. Public parameter names are not schema internals. `key[]` came up in the collection discussion, but the older material did not preserve enough parameter objects to establish the relationship between plain `key` and `key[]`, or to establish whether form, deepObject, and explode came from the same generation point.

## 2023-10-31 review addendum

The review still starts from `internal/api-core-params`'s `v_prev`. The local entry point is:

`src/Laravel/public/swagger-ui/swagger-ui-standalone-preset.js`

This location is retained as a reference point near the parameter declarations. It can help the next review start from the same place, but the filename is not treated as proof that the entire parameter chain belongs there. The fields that still need to be examined are the name, schema, and style fields in the same public parameter object.

This round separated terms that had been conflated in the early draft, leaving only the approaches shown below:

| Object under review | Approach retained at the time |
| --- | --- |
| explicit scalar | Do not rewrite it as a collection first; wait for confirmation from an actual parameter object |
| non-array item | A collection representation can be discussed; this cannot replace the scalar check |
| existing array schema | Treat it as an existing object first, without starting from an assumption of uniform conversion |

The table is not an output contract. It is only there to keep the review from once again treating an existing array schema as an object to be generated.

## Old wording left in place

> Collections can be uniformly collapsed into arrays; scalars can be handled as single-value inputs to arrays.

This sentence was not deleted because it explains why the different shapes were initially grouped together. It is no longer used as a decision. The problem is not that arrays can represent collections, but that this sentence does not distinguish between "a collection being formed from an item" and "an input that already carries an array schema." It also says nothing about public parameter names or serialization styles.

The decision after review remains narrow: do not change an existing array schema first just to obtain a uniform outer shape; new collection representations must be discussed separately from existing objects. The rest remains to be checked against actual parameter objects.

# Parameter Shape History

This page has always been tucked among the old records for the parameter chain. The first few lines mentioned only scalar, collection and array schema, and parameter names, item, style and explode were gradually added in the margins later. They were not a specification written all at once: they include older judgments that were retained, a split introduced by a review, and a normalization approach that was later explicitly crossed out.

These layers are retained below because parameter shape issues did not start becoming complicated at the level of abstract classification. It began with whether a new branch would encounter existing objects, and only later became a question of whether the names, schemas and styles of public parameters could all be explained together.

## 2023-05-24: Original Record

The initial question was a small one: whether existing array schemas could remain in public parameters. At the time both scalar and collection came up in the discussion, so someone proposed putting all three cases under one type of array outer layer. The rationale was straightforward, because if subsequent processing only had to deal with one structure, it appeared to need one fewer level of branching.

The initial draft did not adopt this proposal. This was not because array could not represent collections, but because array schemas were already on the page. If they were treated again as collection structures awaiting generation, the distinction between old and new output would be lost. The earliest recorded judgment went only this far: preserve existing array schemas first; consider explicit scalar cases and newly added collections separately.

That statement had a very narrow scope at the time. It did not explain where parameters were created, nor did it list style combinations. `key`,`key[]`, form, deepObject and explode were all just items to investigate. If these terms had been directly combined into rules at the time, it would have looked more like a finished design on the surface, but would actually have gone beyond what had already been observed.

The initial draft recorded the location to revisit as `v_prev` in `internal/api-core-params`, with `src/Laravel/public/swagger-ui/swagger-ui-standalone-preset.js` as the local entry point. This location was not subsequently removed from the page: it provides a suitable way back in near the parameter declarations, but the early notes did not present it as a complete picture of the implementation.

The three blank items left at the end of the original notes are still there as well: whether existing array schemas were recognized before the collection branch; where the parameter key was obtained; whether the style fields were formed at the same time as the schema. They had no answers at the time.

## Summer 2023: Normalization Draft

The following passage is retained from the first round of consolidation, and its original meaning has not been replaced with later wording:

> collection can be uniformly collapsed into array; scalar can be treated as single-value input to array, leaving only one outer structure to maintain thereafter.

At the time, this was not a careless mistake, but an approach intended to reduce the number of outer types. It focused on how many structures downstream would have to deal with, so it did not list "the input is already an array schema" as a separate condition. Under this approach, scalar could easily be seen as a special case of collection, and existing array schema could easily be seen as an object that still needed to be expanded once more.

The draft did not become a settled decision, but it was not deleted. If only the later branch-based formulation had been retained, readers would mistakenly think that the distinction between "an existing object" and "an object yet to be formed" had been obvious from the start. In fact, it was precisely because this proposal to unify around array could not clearly account for the third category of input that subsequent records gradually broke the problem down.

That period also left behind a misreading: seeing `[]` in a name and immediately classifying the object as a collection. This reading was narrower than unifying around array, but was likewise insufficient. A name can suggest looking further into collection semantics, but cannot by itself explain where the schema came from, much less whether the input was already an array. The old page did not delete this reminder, but only added a question mark next to it.

## 2023-10-31: Review addendum

The review did not produce a set of materials covering all parameters, but instead first changed the order of observation. Rather than first asking "can the parameter be converted to an array", examine these separately: whether a scalar schema is explicitly provided; whether a non-array item schema appears in the collection path; whether the input already has an array schema.

All three relate to parameters, but serve different purposes. For explicit scalar, the concern is whether single-value semantics can retain their own public representation. For non-array item, the concern is whether a collection representation can be formed from an item. For existing array schema, the primary concern is preservation, and it should not automatically be brought into the discussion of "creating a new collection from an item".

During the review, they were placed in the same temporary table, with the following intended meaning:

| Object observed | Misreading to avoid first at the time |
| --- | --- |
| explicit scalar | Do not start by treating it as a collection just to unify the outer layer |
| non-array item | Do not describe the presence of an item as evidence of an existing array |
| existing array schema | Do not reinterpret an already formed object as a collection yet to be generated |

This table only served to stabilize what was being observed, and was not a convention for public output. Nor did it replace the parameter object itself. If the name, schema, style, and explode are not examined together within the same object, the classifications in the table remain easy to misuse.

The review column specifically circles `key`. Earlier records treated it as a field subordinate to the schema, and only later was it recognized as part of the public container. `key[]` likewise cannot be understood solely at face value: it affects how readers interpret collection semantics, but is not enough on its own to determine the branch.

The same round continued by looking back from `src/Laravel/public/swagger-ui/swagger-ui-standalone-preset.js`. This entry point is retained for adjacent navigation and does not support the conclusion that "the entire parameter chain is completed here". The old records reached this point through issue names and call names; the review instead starts here to reconfirm the fields that appear near the parameter object.

## Spring 2024: Notes from a Three-Cell Trial

This section was not compiled into a formal test report, and what remains is a trial note from placing the objects side by side. The cells are still an explicit scalar, a collection with a non-array item, and an existing array schema. The purpose was not to announce complete results for each cell, but to see exactly which cell caused the old unified approach to start conflating objects.

The conclusion from the trial notes was simple: for the first two cells, "where the new representation comes from" can still be discussed, but the third cell cannot be addressed with that same question. An existing array schema is already a public object; if it is still derived from the item using the collection approach, its outer layer will be unwittingly rewritten.

This is not a proof of coverage, nor was it treated as a conclusion about all behavior. It merely provides a more concrete counterexample in support of "preserve the existing array schema first": the presence of the word array in both cases does not mean the same operation is being performed. One is an existing schema, and the other is a collection representation that may be formed from an item.

After the trial notes, a term in the margin was revised to be more precise. "collection" cannot refer both to an array schema already present in the input and to a new collection that needs to be represented by an item. The former describes the state of an existing schema, while the latter describes a path that may form a parameter object. Both objects may be related to array, but they should not override each other.

## Autumn 2024: The Handling Table Retained in Place

The table below was once used to quickly organize the material and retains its original coarse-grained wording:

| Old classification | Old handling |
| --- | --- |
| scalar | Treat as a single-item array |
| collection | Generate an array in all cases |
| array schema | Reprocess as a collection |

This table is now obsolete. Its problem is not just missing fields, but that it erased distinctions in the inputs' source states. Whether the scalar is explicit, whether the item is non-array, and whether the schema is already an array each affect the judgment. The table contains neither parameter names nor styles, so it cannot explain what actually happened to the public container.

Keeping the old table is not meant to send maintainers back to the "uniform array generation" approach, but to preserve the reasons it was later abandoned. If this table were deleted, the early simplification approach would become an oral account with no traceable source; keeping it here lets readers see the exact row where it begins to conflict with preservation.

There was also a narrower older approach during the same period: determine the category solely from the name. It assumed that the mere appearance of `key[]` was enough to show that the parameter should be treated as a collection. This approach is no longer used either. The name is part of the public container, but it is not a complete criterion for identifying the input's source; it must be read alongside the schema, style, and explode of the same parameter.

## Two Additional Remarks from the Review

The review left no complete minutes, and only two brief remarks remain in the margin:

> First treat an existing array schema as an existing object, and do not change it together with newly added collections.

> First align the parameter name and schema; whether you look only at the path or only at the name, neither is enough.

The first remark carries forward the original compatibility trade-off. The second changes the verification method: you cannot infer a collection source just from seeing `key[]`, nor assume that an array schema must have been expanded from a non-array item just because it is an array schema. For a public parameter you must at least read its name, schema and style together in the same object, before you can tell which category of discussion it belongs to.

These two remarks do not say that paths are useless.`src/Laravel/public/swagger-ui/swagger-ui-standalone-preset.js` is still a local entry point, suitable for tracing back from near the declaration. It simply cannot replace the parameter object itself. A file location can provide a starting point for a search, but cannot replace evaluating the fields of the parameter container.

The short-term decision after the review was therefore narrower: an existing array schema is not renamed, reordered or repackaged just because another collection branch exists. It is first identified as input that should be preserved; only after confirming that this is not the case does the discussion move on to whether an item will introduce a collection representation.

## An Explanation That Was Overturned

A later write-up included a claim: as long as the item of a collection is not an array, all related parameters can use the same outer collection layer, with no exception for existing array schema. This claim was later explicitly crossed out.

The reason it was overturned was not that the item schema was unimportant, but that an item can only indicate how the collection branch might be constructed, and cannot erase the fact that the input is already an array. Applying the same construction to an existing array schema would turn "preserving what already exists" into "regenerating it according to another rule". Even if both look like an array, they do not have the same public meaning.

After the correction, this page no longer starts from "every array is the same". Verification first distinguishes existing objects from objects yet to be formed, then discusses the shape of a scalar or an item. This change appears to add only one guard condition, but has actually prevented old array schema from being unintentionally overwritten under the new collection logic.

This also corrected another ambiguous reading in the initial draft: protecting existing array schemas does not mean rejecting all collection representations. The former concerns objects that already exist; the latter can still be discussed for branches outside the explicitly scalar case that have a non-array item. The early wording made "do not harm old objects" sound too much like "do not add collection representations", and this aspect was later corrected.

## Boundaries with adjacent issues

There is also material on placeholder property configuration merge and free-text nested metadata isolation near the parameter chain. These have not been incorporated into this page's decision. The former discusses configuration merging, and the latter discusses nested metadata; what is retained here is the history of the public parameter container shape.

These issues can arise in the same review, but they cannot share a conclusion. Configuration merging may affect whether a schema is visible, but it cannot replace the assessment of whether an existing array schema is protected. Nested metadata isolation also cannot determine which style `key` or `key[]` should have. The proximity of the objects does not mean that a judgment about one can settle a judgment about another.

Therefore, this page does not fold configuration sources, caller handling, or nested metadata into the parameter shape decision. If these objects become blockers during a review, only record that they are blocking the current object, and do not extrapolate new merge rules from the branch descriptions on this page.

## 2025-01-27: Current decision

The preceding raw notes, normalized draft, review addenda, three-cell trial notes, old handling table, and review phrases are all retained here. The current requirement is confined to this one statement:

> OpenApiFilterTrait must keep the public parameter container shape: an explicit scalar schema yields one parameter named by the key with form style and explode=false, while a non-array item schema can also be represented by a key[] parameter whose schema is an array of that item schema with deepObject style and explode=true.

This decision separates two judgments that were initially conflated. An explicit scalar retains a single public parameter named after the key; the collection branch for non-array items can produce a parameter named `key[]`. The two are not substituted for each other merely to achieve the same outer shape.

existing array schema preservation remains a guardrail for the same decision. An existing array schema is not automatically regenerated using the collection branch's representation simply because that branch has a usable representation. The current requirement concerns the public parameter containers for explicit scalar and non-array items; an existing array schema continues to be treated as an already-formed object, unless other local material indicates that it needs to change.

This also relegates the old table's statement "scalar as a single-item array" to a historical proposal. The public representation of an explicit scalar is not renamed to unify its outer shape with the collection branch. Likewise, a collection representation is not determined by its name alone: `key[]`, array schema, deepObject and explode=true must belong to the same corresponding branch, rather than being picked separately from several old records and pieced together into a rule.

The current decision does not adopt three earlier approaches: convert all inputs to array first; determine the parameter category based only on its name; interpret the protection of an existing array schema as a rejection of all collection representations. The first would erase the independent public shape of scalar and also mistake existing objects for new collection inputs. The second ignores schema and style. The third misreads protecting existing objects as refusing to add collection representations.

## Reading diagram added afterward

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> CheckInputObject
    CheckInputObject --> ExplicitScalar : explicit scalar schema
    CheckInputObject --> NonArrayItem : non-array item schema
    CheckInputObject --> ExistingArray : existing array schema
    ExplicitScalar --> SinglePublicParameter
    NonArrayItem --> CollectionPublicParameter
    ExistingArray --> PreserveExistingschema
    SinglePublicParameter --> [*]
    CollectionPublicParameter --> [*]
    PreserveExistingschema --> [*]
```

The diagram was added after the decision as a reading aid and does not replace the decision statements above. It shows an existing array schema as a separate protected branch, rather than as an arrow off the collection branch. This preserves the distinction introduced by the early counterexamples: seeing the same word array does not mean that the same action should be performed.

## Questions still in the margins

Several questions have not yet been moved off this page, but they do not change the current decision.

- Whether parameter name conversion happens before or after the parameter container is formed;
- Whether configuration merging affects the visibility of an explicit schema;
- Which fields need to be retained when an existing array schema also has other fields;
- Whether there is still an adapter layer between the legacy entry point and the subsequent parameter chain that affects only the collection representation.

These questions are kept here because reviewers may encounter them alongside the same parameter object. They are not currently part of the shape decision. Peripheral issues must not be construed as established rules for scalar and non-array item just because configuration or name conversion also comes up during the same review.

## Appendix of Legacy Examples

### Example of Treating a Single Value as a Collection Too

An old note stated: "scalar can also be treated as a single-item array." The focus at the time was to have one fewer type of downstream structure, not to describe public parameters. That sentence did not record key, style, or explode, nor did it state whether a scalar schema was explicitly present.

It is now retained only as a legacy example of the normalization approach. Anyone arriving here from old search results should first see that it belongs to an abandoned approach, and must not extract half a sentence to explain current scalar behavior.

### Example of Expanding an Existing array Again

Another legacy example treated an existing array schema as an ordinary collection, suggesting that another layer of array be generated based on item. This example was later crossed out, but not deleted. It illustrates why preservation must be listed separately: an existing public schema must not be overwritten by another new collection rule.

The legacy example did not include a usable actual parameter object, and should not be treated as reproduction steps. It remains in the appendix, only to explain why the judgment that "every array is the same" arose in the past.

### Example of Going by the Name First

There is also a margin note that says "treat it as a collection upon seeing `key[]`". This line is likewise no longer applicable. The name is part of the public container, not a complete criterion for determining the input source. It can prompt reviewers to look further at the schema and style, but it cannot determine the branch on its own.

## End-of-Page Review Checkpoints

When reviewing this history, continue to start from `internal/api-core-params`, `v_prev`, and `src/Laravel/public/swagger-ui/swagger-ui-standalone-preset.js`. First confirm whether the current object is an existing array schema, an explicit scalar, or a collection with a non-array item; then check the parameter name, schema, style, and explode together in the same public parameter object.

If only the old text about a uniform array representation is found, it should be read in the context of the abandoned approach. If an existing array schema is found, first record it as an object to preserve. If an explicit scalar or non-array item is found, then determine its public shape according to the current decision.

Start by testing a narrower assumption: when a parameter placeholder provides properties, feed those properties into the filter's configuration entry point; leave free-text nested metadata out of that entry point for now. # Placeholder Property Merge Proposal

The initial draft treated placeholder properties and free-text nested as the same configuration problem, but that claim didn't hold up on review. The first is about whether existing configuration gets lost when the property list enters the filter; the second is about whether nested metadata crosses its own boundary. The two can arise together, but they can't be validated together through a single merge path.

The approach we're keeping for the trial does not treat placeholder properties as a one-shot replacement for filter state. If existing property configuration is overwritten, a previously working filter will change behavior because a new set of lists was added at the parameter entry point. The smaller change is to bring the lists in as supplemental information and pass the parameter's filter context to the configuration process along with them.

Another earlier idea has been dropped for now: flatten the metadata from nested free-text into the parent, then let property configuration consume it all. This looks like it could remove one level of branching, but it doesn't explain why nested and parent relationships are interchangeable. We now treat free-text nested metadata isolation only as a separate review item; don't document it as a side effect of the merge proposal until it's confirmed.

The trade-offs listed then are still useful:

- Replacement-based configuration makes the final set of properties easy to see, but obscures what the filter originally contained.
- Additive configuration preserves the existing content, but requires making clear at which step the parameter context is introduced.
- Giving nested metadata its own boundary adds another entry point, but prevents decisions about parent properties from spilling over into nested input.

The rollback conditions have also been made more specific: if review finds that existing property configuration is no longer retained after adding the placeholder, or that nested metadata is interpreted by the parent configuration, stop this trial and return to the original configuration path. `src/Laravel/public/swagger-ui-bundle.js` remains a lookup starting point in the old records; it only helps locate the name used at the time and cannot replace runtime verification of the parameters.

# Placeholder Property Merge Proposal

This record originally framed the problem too much like a metadata cleanup: get the placeholder's properties, process them uniformly, and cover free-text nested along the way. That starting point has been left in place because several later reviews have still found this page using the same set of terms; it should no longer be treated as a complete proposal.

> Previous proposal (retained): First expand nested free-text as part of the parent property, then pass a configuration to the filter again. This gives properties a single entry point.
>
> This proposal was later abandoned. It did not explain the boundary between the parent property and nested metadata, and it did not preserve the configuration the filter already carried.

The first discussion focused on whether the placeholder could enumerate properties. That question was too narrow. Even if the list itself was correct, writing the configuration directly could still erase the filter's existing property information; replacement writes would also lose the parameter context. Only after a follow-up review considered these two risks together did the candidate approach change from "generate a new configuration" to "add information to the existing configuration."

free-text nested should be considered separately. It is not an ancillary field of placeholder properties, nor can it share a processing branch just because both go through parameter metadata. Early notes assumed that once the property merge was correct, nested behavior would naturally stabilize as well; that assumption no longer applies. The only conclusion retained is that nested metadata needs its own isolation boundary, and the parent property configuration cannot substitute for checking that boundary.

## Approaches Compared at the Time

**Replace the configuration.** The placeholder list forms a new property configuration, which is then passed to the filter. The advantage is a straightforward path, with the resulting list easy to see in the logs. The downside is that the new list obscures the existing configuration, making it hard to tell during a regression whether the placeholder was missing entries or the old content was already gone.

**Append to the configuration.** Preserve the filter's existing property configuration, and include the placeholder list and parameter filter context in the same configuration operation. This requires more care with the order of writes to the configuration object, but avoids having the parameter entry point replace the entire previous state. This direction is retained.

**Fold nested metadata into the parent.** This was the simplification in the old proposal. It reduces the apparent number of branches, but treats "whether nested input is independent" as settled by default. There is not enough justification for that assumption, so this approach is not being adopted.

The requirement finalized in this round is: When a parameter placeholder lists properties, ParameterExtensionTrait must configure a PropertyAwareFilterInterface by merging every listed property and the parameter filter context into, rather than replacing, the filter's existing property configuration.

This statement corrects the earlier position on replacing the configuration; it does not mean that all processing details for nested free-text have already been defined. In particular, when the placeholder lists no properties, when the target filter does not provide this interface, and when nested metadata and the parent appear together, the actual entry points still need to be checked individually. Do not use the result from one branch to draw a conclusion about another.

Rollback is also limited to this trial: if the old configuration is not preserved after properties are added, or if parent property processing takes nested metadata outside its own boundary, back out the append path, restore the original configuration, and reconfirm the handoff point for the parameter context. Here, "restore" does not mean rolling back the entire parameter chain, only backing this proposal out of property configuration.

The earlier investigation started at `src/Laravel/public/swagger-ui-bundle.js`. It is useful for finding the names used at the time and nearby references, not for determining implementation ownership. When this old proposal is referenced, first establish whether the investigation is about placeholder property configuration merge or free-text nested metadata isolation; the two share historical background here, but no longer share a conclusion.

Still unresolved:

- the visibility scope of parameter filter context within the existing configuration object;
- whether to keep using the original configuration when there is no property list;
- whether the isolation point for nested free-text is before metadata construction or filter dispatch.

These questions remain at the bottom of the page so that next time, unconfirmed nested behavior is not presented as something the property merge has already resolved.

# UUID/ULID compatibility check workflow

This page was originally a very short migration checklist. UUID, ULID, and default query parameters were listed together mainly because legacy callers would supply these materials in the same round of changes. On review, the original "schema output confirmed" assessment does not cover the subsequent validation results or default-value reads, so the old assessment is retained below, with a separate sequence that can be checked.

## Legacy entry point from 2023

The migration starts at `src/JsonSchema/Metadata/Property/Factory/SchemaPropertyMetadataFactory.php`. This entry point is useful for finding schema property metadata; it is not a migration table that can replace caller records. Nearby names include `Schema`, `ApiProperty`, `PropertyNotFoundException`, and `PropertyMetadataFactoryInterface`. An exception when a property is missing cannot simply be recorded as rejection of the UUID or ULID format.

Only three steps were recorded at the time: take a parameter declaration snippet from a legacy caller, inspect the generated schema, then put the results in the checklist. Whether the input was a single value or a collection was not recorded separately, nor was a separate copy kept of each of the two ways of specifying default query parameters.

```text
Legacy caller parameters
      |
      v
schema snippet
      |
      v
Checklist
```

This diagram records only how the early materials were arranged. It does not prove that work on both the schema and validation sides was complete.

## Review margin notes from 2024

The review opened with a practical question: could the migration be checked off if a format name appeared in the schema? At the time, no validation-side output was available to match it, so this item was split into two columns. The first column records only the schema snippet; the second awaits results from a runnable validation check. Without the second column, no longer write "parameters validated".

The same review also noted that single-value and collection parameters cannot share a row. Even if the only difference between their inputs is the collection form, the migration record must retain both original inputs. This does not assume that they will necessarily produce different results; it prevents one sample from standing in for the other.

Default query parameters are handled separately. The old page had two default forms, but there was not enough material to establish that the same caller would read them in the same way. Keep one row for each form: save the original parameter syntax before migration, then read each form's metadata after migration. Leave the row with no input blank; do not fill it with the other form.

## An unfinished attempt

There was an attempt to inspect the schema first, then infer validation results from the format. Only schema-side observations were retained, with no validation output that could be reviewed again. This approach was not carried forward as a migration step, but it is retained here because it explains why the old record equated "has a format" with "complete".

The same round also included an attempt to change the default query parameters first and look for the old input afterward. This produced no known code-level result, but it would lose the pre-migration default forms. Rolling back would then mean reconstructing them from memory alone. The order was therefore changed to save the old input first, then read the post-migration metadata.

## Existing checklist

| Item | Keep before migration | Review after migration |
| --- | --- | --- |
| UUID single value | Original parameter input | schema snippet, validation-side results |
| UUID collection | Separate collection input | schema snippet, validation-side results |
| ULID | Original parameter input | schema snippet, validation-side results |
| Default form 1 | Original syntax | Corresponding metadata |
| Default form 2 | Original syntax | Corresponding metadata |

"Form 1" and "form 2" in the table are only archival labels, not new interface names. The caller's original parameter syntax should still be copied as written. If only the schema is available for an item, leave the validation-side results as not obtained; if only one default form is available, do not mark the other as having the same result.

## Rollback notes

When the old path needs to be restored, first restore the legacy caller's parameter declaration and the default form originally used. Replay the single-value and collection inputs for UUID and ULID separately; save each schema snippet first, then add the validation-side results. Read metadata separately for the two default query parameter forms as well; do not use one request as a substitute for the two old inputs.

If you encounter `PropertyNotFoundException` during restoration, put the exception and the property that triggered it in the same diagnostic entry. The old materials do not document the full set of exception branches, so only the point at which reading stopped can be recorded here; do not expand that into a format validation failure.

## Questions still unanswered

There is still no evidence establishing whether the two default query forms ultimately reach the same processing point, nor a complete record of all behavior when a property is missing. These two gaps remain open in the migration checklist for now.

# UUID/ULID Compatibility Check Workflow

This page began as a narrow table used on site during the migration, then grew longer through several rounds of added notes. Do not treat the old sequence at the beginning as the current basis for sign-off: it only shows what materials people had at hand early on, and which areas they did not investigate further at the time.

## 2023-06-26: Record the entry point first

The earliest record started with `src/JsonSchema/Metadata/Property/Factory/SchemaPropertyMetadataFactory.php`. Near the top of the file, you can see `Schema`, `ApiProperty`, `PropertyNotFoundException` and `PropertyMetadataFactoryInterface`. Its purpose at the time was very limited: navigate from parameter declarations to schema property metadata, then copy the partial output they saw back to the migration page.

That page grouped UUID, ULID and default query parameters together. This was because these types of material would all appear for legacy callers during a single migration, not because they had already been proven to be handled in the same place. At the time, the person keeping the record used only two columns, "Format" and "Default value", without separating single values from collections or saving the validation-side results.

```text
Legacy caller parameter declaration
        |
        v
schema fragment
        |
        v
Migration complete
```

This old diagram is still retained. The last arrow reflects the working habits of that time, not a judgment to adopt going forward.

The brief rule at the time was: check the schema for UUID, and also make a note of the ULID being inspected; if the parameter looks like a collection, add a sentence in the same format cell; if the default value appears to have been left out, keep moving forward. The record did not say where each of the two default query forms came from. It can help later readers find the old entry point, but it cannot reconstruct the full migration outcome.

## 2024-01: Reminders in the margin

A year later, a sentence was added: "format is not the same as a constraint." This sentence had no accompanying examples and did not change the number of columns in the original table, so for a while it remained only a marginal note. It at least pointed out the gap in the old table: a schema fragment answers whether a description was written out, while whether the validation side generated an executable object is a separate matter.

The same page still contains the statement that "default values will merge on their own". This was a working assumption at the time, not a confirmed interface rule. The statement did not specify which type of caller input supplied the default values, nor did it answer whether the two legacy forms were interchangeable. It is retained so as not to erase the origins of the subsequent changes; it is no longer used as a basis for migration.

The review also moved the single-value and collection cases into separate rows. The reason for the split was simple: when you have only one sample, you cannot treat the collection form as the single-value form by default. The pre-migration input should be kept as is, and the post-migration schema fragment should be saved separately. If only one side is available, the table can remain incomplete.

## 2024-02-21: The table retained after review

This review did not require cataloging all callers, only that the person performing the migration be able to describe the one input they checked. The table was changed to the following format:

| Item recorded | Old material | New material |
| --- | --- | --- |
| UUID single value | Single-value parameter input | schema and validation-side results |
| UUID collection | Collection parameter input | schema and validation-side results |
| ULID | Original parameter input | schema and validation-side results |
| Default query form one | Old syntax | metadata read after migration |
| Default query form two | Old syntax | metadata read after migration |

"Form one" and "form two" are just placeholders in the table. They are not interfaces created by renaming callers. Whichever syntax the person performing the migration already has, place that syntax beside the corresponding record; when no sample is available mark it as not obtained, and do not fill it in based on the name.

From this point on, the schema side and the validation side are no longer combined under a single "format is valid" label. Having a schema fragment only shows that material has been obtained on the schema side; if there are no validation-side results, leave the status at not obtained. This stopping point looks worse than the old table, but it preserves the actual gaps.

## Spring 2024: Failed shortcuts

An earlier attempt tried first to work backward from the format in the schema to infer that validation had already been generated. No validation output was retained at the time, only a schema fragment, so this shortcut did not provide a result that could be rechecked. It was later made explicit that "the schema has format" would no longer be used as a substitute for observations on the validation side.

Another shortcut was to first combine the two default query forms into one default value, then go back and check metadata. It saved one row of records, but left no original form available for rollback. The sequence was then changed to: first save the old forms, then read metadata for each after migration; only when both results are available, discuss whether they behave the same.

These two attempts were not documented as incidents. The only known fact was that the material was insufficient, and a missing column could not be used to infer an implementation defect. The earlier page still retains the "continue after checking schema" paragraph, and has a "deprecated" marker added nearby, making it easy to recognize it as the old procedure.

## 2024-06: Operator's margin notes

During migration, first locate the parameter declarations of the legacy callers. UUID or ULID If it is a single value, mark it separately; if it is a collection, save the collection input separately. Do not combine the two into one sample just to make the table look neat.

Next, retrieve the relevant snippets through the schema property metadata entry point. What must remain is the parameter-related format, scalar or collection shape, and the OpenAPI parameter description; there is no need to move the entire output into the page. Names such as `Schema`, `ApiProperty`, and so on next to the file are merely objects encountered during location.

Then retrieve the validation-side results. The results should show whether executable constraints were generated; if they cannot be retrieved for now, write "pending retrieval." Do not treat format names appearing in schema as evidence that this field is complete.

Handle default query parameters afterward. First save the old form, then read the migrated metadata. Keep the inputs and results for the two forms separately; do not merge them first, nor let one result stand in for the other.

## 2025-05: Gaps left by a caller walkthrough

A later walkthrough reviewed the "pre-migration input" and "post-migration output" together again. The old page sometimes contained only a result snippet, without its corresponding input; at other times, it contained only one default query form. The walkthrough record therefore requires the parameter declaration actually used to remain in the pre-migration column, with schema and validation-side results kept separately in the post-migration column.

If a reader following the old instructions gets only as far as schema, record that it stopped at schema; if there is no validation-side material, do not write it up as a successful review; if only one default form was read, leave the other blank. This blank reflects the actual state of the work, not something that may be filled with a similar sample.

There is also no complete branch for the missing property scenario. When `PropertyNotFoundException` is encountered, at minimum place the triggering property, the input at that time, and the snippets already obtained together. Without these objects, it is impossible to determine which step the exception actually obscured.

## 2025-09 to 2025-10: Two cards separate the entry points

The review item for APC-204 requires preserving the inputs that directly trigger UUID and ULID schema validation, as well as the tool's actual output. The public record also left a reminder that "one item remains unconfirmed" and required the input and output to be placed in the pre- and post-migration caller review records. It did not provide complete implementation ownership for this page, so here it is treated only as a verification entry point.

The caller walkthrough for APC-221 focuses on dual default query forms. The walkthrough did not prove that the two default query forms are equivalent; it only brought both forms back into the review. If a reader sees only one of them, they should record that the other was not covered, rather than automatically merging the two rows.

The two cards serve different purposes: the former is a reminder to save the original inputs and outputs needed for format validation, while the latter is a reminder to walk through the default forms separately. Neither should be rewritten as a new parameter name. The migration page still takes the forms actually used by legacy callers as its source of truth.

## Explicit Corrections to the Previous Approach

The statement in an earlier paragraph that "you can proceed when the schema includes format" is now outdated. It can still serve as a first-pass way to spot missing schema descriptions, but it cannot serve as a sign that the entire parameter chain is complete.

"Default values will merge automatically" is also retained as a historical position, not as the current procedure. The available material is insufficient to prove that it applies to both legacy forms. The current approach is to retain both legacy inputs and read the post-migration metadata for each separately; without results for both, do not discuss merging or interchanging them.

The following old sequence is no longer used either: first change the default query parameters, then fill in the pre-migration inputs from memory at the end. This would lose the original forms needed for rollback, so it has been marked as outdated in the margin. When restoring the old path, start with the saved inputs rather than working backward from the new page to reconstruct the old state.

## Migration Worksheet

### What to Save First

1. Obtain the original parameter declarations from legacy callers, without changing parameter names or replacing UUID or ULID samples with ordinary strings.
2. Mark whether the input is a single value, a collection, or one of the default query forms.
3. Save the original pre-migration form. For default query forms, do not save only the merged values.
4. Obtain the schema fragment related to the parameters via `src/JsonSchema/Metadata/Property/Factory/SchemaPropertyMetadataFactory.php`.

### What to Obtain Next

5. Store schema-side results separately from validation-side results. A schema fragment cannot replace results from executable constraints.
6. For UUID and ULID, retain separate results for single values and collections, and do not put collection records into single-value cells.
7. Read the post-migration metadata separately for each of the two default query forms. Leave cells without actual read results marked as not obtained.
8. Have someone who was not involved in the changes perform a caller review following the original instructions. Record whether they stop at the legacy inputs, schema, validation side, or default-value retrieval.

The ordering here serves the migration documentation, and does not require redrawing the call relationships for the entire factory. Paths are only entry points for locating schema property metadata; adjacent names seen in a file do not automatically form a causal chain from input to validation.

## Current completion criteria

The UUID/ULID format contract spans schema and validation: UuidFilter publishes scalar and collection UUID alternatives and both id and id[] OpenAPI parameters, while string schemas with uuid or ulid format create exactly the corresponding executable validation constraint.

Under these criteria, the scalar and collection forms of UUID must be checked separately. `id` and `id[]` are two distinct OpenAPI parameter records, and cannot be collapsed into a single parameter slot. String schemas with the `uuid` or `ulid` format also need a corresponding executable validation constraint; with only schema fragments, the migration documentation is still incomplete.

These criteria do not replace the checks for default query parameters. Each of the two default forms must still retain its own pre-migration input, and obtain its own post-migration metadata. The caller walkthrough must show which form is actually read; if one item is missing, retain the gap, and do not fill it with the other item's results.

## Rolling back to the old path

Rollback starts with the old caller's original input. First restore the original parameter declaration, then restore the default query form it uses. Do not first merge the two default forms into a single new value, because doing so would make it impossible to confirm which path has been restored for the old caller.

For rollback of UUID and ULID, use single-value or collection input respectively, reread the relevant schema fragments, and then record the validation-side results. At a minimum, the rollback documentation must be able to match up the old input, schema, validation-side results, and metadata for the default query form. If an item is missing, identify which item is missing, and do not plug the gap with another item's successful result.

If you encounter `PropertyNotFoundException` during rollback, keep the exception together with the property, input, and materials already obtained. It only indicates that this read encountered a missing property; the available materials do not describe a more complete failure branch, so it cannot simply be described as UUID, ULID, or a migration failure for the default forms.

When reviewing callers after restoration, continue to walk through single values, collections, and each of the two default forms separately. If only the schema has been restored for an item, with no validation-side results, leave that item pending collection. Reverting does not mean reverting only the default values or only the schema; differences left on either side will leave the next comparison without a reference point.

## Review excerpts

One recurring question in reviews is: whether caller migration can be deemed complete based only on schema changes. The current records do not make that determination this way. Schema snippets can show that some descriptive-layer materials have been obtained, but they cannot replace executable constraints on the validation side, nor can they replace metadata reads for the two default query forms.

Another question is: whether `PropertyNotFoundException` should be classified as a format validation failure. The records do not classify it this way. First save the triggering property and the input present at the time, then check what has been obtained for the schema, the validation side, and the default forms separately. When materials from the time of the exception are unavailable, the page retains only the exception name and the stopping point.

The review did not require listing all callers, nor did it require inferring the internal convergence point from parameter names. Reviewed calls Fang Ke may include the original inputs and outputs; do not describe callers that have not been reviewed as compatible. Whether the two default forms ultimately share a single processing location remains a related issue.

## Related issues not yet split out

There are currently not enough local records to determine whether the two default query forms ultimately converge at the same processing location. This question does not prevent migration materials from being saved as two rows, nor should it be answered prematurely by the old claim that "default values will merge on their own". If an actual metadata comparison is obtained later, add a separate assessment then.

There are also no complete samples for the missing-property exception branch. The current page only specifies that the exception, property, input, and any schema or validation-side materials already obtained must be kept together at the time. Do not invent uniform error behavior just to make the migration table look complete.

`DOC-16` is a related validation design record. You can navigate from here when you need to compare validation-side details captured at the time, but it does not replace this page's pre-migration inputs and rollback materials. APC-204 and APC-221 still point to the format validation walkthrough and the walkthrough of the two default forms, respectively.

## Appendix: Old examples still retained

### Old example one: Looking only at the schema

The old quick-check method is to see whether schema contains a format name. It is suitable for detecting missing descriptions, but cannot sign off on the validation side or on the default query forms. Do not delete the old example, because this is how the early migration pages worked; when using it now, add the note "schema check only" next to it.

### Old example 2: Stuff a collection into a single-value cell

Early tables wrote collection inputs after the single-value record. This looked like it saved a line, but later it was impossible to determine whether the collection form had its own schema or validation-side result. This example is no longer used, but the original paragraph remains as historical reference.

### Old example 3: Default values merge on their own

"Default values will merge on their own" was an old working assumption. It explains why only one default form was stored at the time; it is not part of the current migration rules. Now retain the original input and the metadata read result for each of the two forms; when actual results are missing, do not judge them equivalent.

### Minimum review order

```text
Original caller input
      |
      +--> schema fragment
      |
      +--> validation-side result
      |
      +--> metadata for default query form one
      |
      +--> metadata for default query form two
```

This diagram only indicates the objects in the migration materials that must be stored separately. It does not indicate that these objects are generated sequentially by the same code block, nor does it replace live output.

One unresolved item remains at the end: the current record still cannot explain every manifestation of a missing property. After the actual input and the error context are obtained, add it next to the corresponding fallback record.

title: Partial Search Dispatch Troubleshooting Tree

versions.body:
# Partial Search Dispatch Troubleshooting Tree

Symptoms: With a partial search on the same query parameter, changing only the input's case changes the result set; another reported issue is that free-text doesn't seem to cover the expected property. Keep these two symptoms separate to start with, because the first can at least be traced to the comparison result, while in the second there is often no record of which property was actually targeted.

First record the property name and input value from the request, then open `src/Doctrine/Orm/Filter/SearchFilter.php`. This investigation only covers the search conditions received by SearchFilter; don't start by working backward from the resource definition, and don't guess whether the configuration took effect based on the result count.

## partial branch

If the property is known and the issue only occurs with inputs that differ in case, follow the old guidance and treat it as a database-side difference. SearchFilter is only responsible for passing the partial conditions into the search; case handling should not get a separate check at the property layer. Then check whether the two requests for the same property both took the same search path; if they did, stop here and do not add separate configuration for case-sensitive partial search.

If the request doesn't specify a property, or the corresponding name cannot be found in the configuration, stop here. Do not substitute results from another field or treat a hit from free-text as proof that partial is working correctly. Record whether the name is missing from the request or the configuration, and wait for the caller to fill it in before returning to this branch.

## free-text branch

The old approach treated free-text as a single unified search: the property configuration determined which fields could be matched, but did not change the dispatch entry point. So first determine whether a particular property was left out or the entire request never reached SearchFilter. In the first case, only check whether that property appears in the existing configuration; in the second, go back to the request parameters themselves. Do not add default fields inside the filter.

If the same request shows a case-related difference in partial search and someone also asks to split free-text by property, keep two separate records to start with. Here, per-property free-text dispatch is not treated as independent behavior; the assessment at the time was that it still used the unified entry point. If there is no sample request that identifies a specific property, stop changing the configuration.

The scope of this record ends at SearchFilter. If you need to confirm what the caller actually passed in, start a separate check; do not work backward from the returned results.

# Filter Property and Anchored Search Compatibility Workflow

This page originally treated the two symptoms as a single migration: find `src/Doctrine/Orm/Filter/SearchFilter.php` from the issue name or call name, then continue by reviewing the declarations near the file. This entry point is still useful, but it only answers "where to start looking"; it does not answer "which call caused what result." The old wording is retained here and is not being turned into a current rule.

## Entry point changes

The old record followed this path:

```text
missing filter property failure
        ↓
issue name / call name
        ↓
SearchFilter.php
```

During verification, use the file path as the stable anchor and treat the call as a second object. The adjacent relationships visible in the file header are: `ApiPlatform\Doctrine\Common\Filter\SearchFilterInterface`, `ApiPlatform\Doctrine\Common\Filter\SearchFilterTrait`, `ApiPlatform\Doctrine\Orm\Util\QueryBuilderHelper`, and `ApiPlatform\Doctrine\Orm\Util\QueryNameGeneratorInterface`. These names are used only to confirm the local reading scope and are not enough to replace an actual call.

Keep the legacy filter property and query parameter, along with the shape of the existing filter contract. The migration is about the verification entry point and recording method, not changing caller parameters through this page. When callers continue to use the original entry point, first record the property they pass in, then record the final result they see; do not fill in the intervening relationship based only on the file name or error label.

## Discrepancies left during review

The observation recorded under `APC-209` is that the output for missing filter property cannot be reproduced consistently. The early path therefore tended to produce a premature judgment—that as long as `SearchFilter.php` could be located, the failure point had been found. Later review did not use that judgment. Each review must record separately the "missing property," the "query parameter that triggered it," and "whether the output actually appeared"; if any one of these has no original result, stop at that item.

`APC-226` records another kind of gap: a particular use of anchored search shows abnormal behavior, but the most recent actual call and the result seen by the user need to be added back. The anchored boundary here cannot be inferred from the issue title. First save the search value and property used in the call, then record which side the result landed on; without the original call artifact, retain only "actual call pending," and do not turn a guess into a compatibility conclusion.

## Migrate in batches by symptom

The first batch handles missing property. Start with the legacy investigation name, then return to the file path and check the local interfaces, traits, and adjacent items related to the query builder. If the output can be reproduced, record the missing property and the error seen by the user; if it cannot, retain the "unstable" state described by APC-209, and do not let one successful run overwrite one failed run.

The second batch handles anchored search. Using the same file entry, find the actual call, but do not carry the failure output from the first batch into the second. Record the search value, property, and boundary result seen by the user. If only the issue name is found and no call form, stop the migration at the old entry point and wait for the original call to be added back before continuing.

The two batches share files but not judgments. `SearchFilterInterface` and `SearchFilterTrait` can only indicate the local declarations to revisit; `QueryBuilderHelper` and `QueryNameGeneratorInterface` can only be used for adjacent navigation. They cannot by themselves prove that missing property has been triggered, nor can they by themselves prove the boundary behavior of anchored search.

## Return to the old entry point

The old path remains suitable for records without a stable output: issue name or call name → `SearchFilter.php`. If checking along the new path does not recover the original call, first return to this record path; do not delete the old judgment, only note alongside it which item was not rechecked. Calls and outputs already found remain on the new path, to avoid writing the new results back over an old record located only by name.

The verification design for `DOC-21` is nearby, but this page retains only the migration entry point, compatible calls, and the two historical symptoms. Specific implementation relationships still need to be checked against the corresponding code references and actual calls; this page does not turn callers, outputs, or recovery results that have not yet been obtained into conclusions.
