# Doctrine Quality Signal Dashboard Legacy Entry Migration Index

This index preserves the work order used when the Doctrine Quality Signal Dashboard originally split its entry points. It focuses on failure samples, regression stratification, and unstable-signal attribution, not on collecting all Doctrine-related pages into one directory. The legacy entry, replacement location, and callers that may still use it are recorded separately; the field for cases where the original record cannot be found remains blank.

The original plan was to continue using `release regression`. Later, we tried to split out `query parameter` because their failure paths differ: the former makes it easier to place samples into regression stratification, while the latter is closer to the conditions supplied by the caller for that invocation. This split does not mean the legacy entry has already been retired.

```text
Legacy entry: current entry-legacy entry migration index
   ├── release regression
   │      └── Legacy samples are still reviewed from here
   ├── query parameter
   │      └── Replacement location for a limited trial
   └── metadata factory
          └── Listed as the second candidate at the time, not yet treated as the default entry
```

## What Remains from Before the Migration

Start with `docs/adj-doctrine/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`. First record the version, consumers, inputs, and first failure result visible through the original entry. Here, "consumer" means a person or process that can still obtain the quality signal through the old path, not a project whose name has appeared in the directory.

If all you have is a cleaned-up screenshot of a successful result, do not migrate yet. It cannot show whether the original input will still trigger the same type of failure after passing through the replacement location, nor whether the second call preserves the same state. Legacy samples should remain with the legacy entry, and new trial results should be recorded separately, so that when revisiting we are not left with only a conclusion that has already been cleaned up.

## Migrate One Path First

Switch only one known consumer at a time from the legacy entry to `query parameter`. The other consumers do not follow automatically just because their names match. During the trial, keep the legacy entry readable; compare the results and errors for the same input at both locations, as well as the state after a second call. Do not change the input, parameter syntax, and attribution method at the same time.

`metadata factory` was also listed as a candidate at the time. It is suitable for handling some parameter-related lookups, but there is no evidence that it already covers the uses of `OpenAPI schema`, so it must not be written up as the sole entry point once migration is complete. This gap remains in the index.

## Return to the Legacy Entry

Stop switching if any of the following occurs: the content returned by the replacement location cannot be matched to the legacy sample; the original input cannot be replayed; or the consumer cannot find the earlier signal at the new location. To restore, first switch that consumer back to the legacy entry, then check once using the original input. Do not use a sample cleaned up later to replace the initial record.

While the legacy entry remains in place, samples for `release regression` are still looked up according to the original stratification. Keeping records in both the old and new locations does not mean they are synchronized; the completion status of a migration batch is confirmed only by the actual consumers.

## Handoff Point

The file we can currently locate is still `docs/adj-doctrine/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`. Some older notes in it word `metadata factory` too close to the default path; that was only the candidate assessment at the time. If a caller is confirmed later, add a note beside the corresponding legacy entry and replacement location; do not overwrite the original failure samples.

# Quality Signal Desk Legacy Entry Migration Index

This page preserves a migration thread that was never fully cleaned up. Quality Signal Desk initially started from Doctrine failure samples, and later handled regression stratification, unstable signal attribution, and parameter entry points in different locations. The index itself did not become a unified entry point: it merely puts old paths, alternative locations, and the consumers that had been mentioned together, making it easier to find the starting point while old records are still being referenced.

The file location remains `docs/adj-doctrine/migration/current-entry-legacy-entry-migration-index.md`. The page name was not renamed along with the migration batches, so seeing "current entry" in the directory does not prove that it represents the path currently in use. This name was once only intended to keep existing links from breaking.

## Original split

The first version treated `release regression` as the mainline. At that time, failure samples were mainly reviewed by regression stratification, while parameters were merely notes attached alongside the samples. A different approach later appeared: expose `query parameter` separately so that callers could retrieve that signal by the conditions passed in. The two lines had different failure exits, so the latter approach was not directly inserted into the former path at the time.

The old notes also marked `metadata factory` as a candidate alternative location. That passage is retained below because it explains why some consumers jumped there from the index:

> If parameter-related lookup has been separated from sample stratification, try `metadata factory` first; keep the old entry readable, then decide whether to clean it up after confirmation.

This is not the current conclusion. That trial did not prove that `metadata factory` covered all consumers, and in particular did not confirm the actual destination of `OpenAPI schema`. Treating it as the default entry would erase the consumer scope that had not been filled in at the time.

```text
Early review

Current entry-Legacy entry migration index
        │
        ├── release regression ──> failed samples in regression stratification
        │
        ├── query parameter ────> separately trialed parameter entry
        │
        └── metadata factory ───> candidate location, full adoption not confirmed

Rollback: trial consumer ──> legacy entry
```

The diagram above only shows the relationships retained at that time. It does not indicate who has completed migration, nor does it indicate that the outputs from the three locations are necessarily identical.

## Notation for a migration batch

The old path was not removed all at once. Each batch first finds a still-identifiable consumer in the index file, then records which line it originally followed to find the signal. If the consumer entered through `release regression`, retain the corresponding sample's stratification position; if it needs to be reproduced by the conditions passed in, leave a trial record under `query parameter`. When both records exist, do not retain only the one that is easier to read later.

| Object in the batch | Handling at the time | Resulting state |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Legacy entry | Remains readable for checking the original samples and original links | Does not mean someone still uses it |
| `release regression` | Retain failure samples from regression stratification | Cannot replace the trial results for the parameter entry |
| `query parameter` | Connect only one consumer for comparison | Do not change the input and attribution at the same time during comparison |
| `metadata factory` | Serve as a candidate location | The scope of `OpenAPI schema` has not been confirmed |

This round of comparison changes only the entry conditions. The original input, version, and first failure result must remain next to the old record; otherwise, when the alternative location looks normal, it is impossible to tell whether the migration succeeded or the comparison object changed. The state of the second call must also be recorded, because an identical first result does not mean that subsequent queries still follow the same path.

Early records once required, "Stop maintaining the old entry as soon as the new entry appears." That statement is no longer applicable. A name appearing in a directory, document, or display page can only prove that the page has been reorganized; it cannot prove that the original consumers have migrated from the old path. Before actually closing it out, you must at least be able to map the consumer, old entry, and alternative location. Entries that cannot be mapped should continue to be retained according to the old records; do not use the new name to fill them in as migrated.

## Trying the alternative location from the old entry

1. Find the sample or call description under the old entry in the index file, and note the original input and version.
2. Determine whether the consumer actually depends on regression stratification; if so, review it first along `release regression`. Do not skip the sample layer just because parameter wording appears.
3. Only when lookup by call conditions is needed should you connect the same consumer to `query parameter`. This step changes only the entry; do not simultaneously rewrite the parameters, sample, or attribution.
4. Compare the results, errors, and states after another call for the old entry and the trial line. If the alternative line lacks a record corresponding to the original input, stop the batch here.
5. Write the consumers that can still be confirmed next to their respective entries. The index does not replace the caller's own records; it only preserves the connection points that need to be revisited during migration.

This order came from the trial practices at the time and remains useful as a reference, but not every path that appeared later can be migrated this way. In particular, for old links with only display text and no original failure sample, you cannot infer from the name whether they belong to `release regression` or `query parameter`.

## Things retained during rollback

When the alternative location does not match the old sample, first connect the trial consumer back to the old entry. After restoration, replay the original input and retain the versions and results from before and after restoration. Do not delete the trial line: it shows what was compared and can prevent the same inconsistency from being treated as a new issue next time.

The old version described restoring the old entry as a simple reverse operation, but later this proved insufficient. If the input or sample stratification was also changed during the trial, reconnecting the entry does not mean that the original state has been restored. In that case, first restore the old relationship, then put the changed conditions back into the original record one by one. Entries without the original input can only be marked as unverified; do not close them out based on one successful display.

Regarding the exit action, the index initially did not clearly document the intermediate process. APCD-002 later supplemented the gap before and after the execution record: the records at both ends can be matched, while the middle value remains empty. This gap was not filled into a definite step by subsequent documentation, so it still should not be interpreted as "rollback completed."

The records for APCD-003 also invalidated the original download step. The exit entry and the execution record have different hash values, and the download entry has been disabled; afterward, the discrepancy remained attached to the download record. # GraphQL Legacy Entry Migration Index

This index retains the migration guidance used by GraphQl · Performance Lab at the time. The lab works on capacity baselines, resource curves, and degradation localization; a legacy entry is not merely a directory alias. Callers still using it can send the same input to different failure exits. Therefore, a new entry appearing in the directory cannot be considered migration complete.

At the time, two paths were compared side by side: continue organizing under `query parameter`, or split `OpenAPI schema` out on its own. Do not use it as grounds to remove all legacy entries at once.

During migration, first find a replacement location for each legacy entry in the index, then confirm which part of the input the caller actually uses. Once one is confirmed, retain the correspondence record for the old and new entries; do not fold similarly named side paths into the same batch. The observed `nested relation` is only a lead for this batch; it cannot replace checking other relations. List entries involving `validation constraint` separately: it may be recorded alongside the new location, but at the time there was no evidence that the legacy callers had completed the replacement.

# Doctrine On-Call Discrepancy Review

This anomaly occurred during an on-call window for the Doctrine adapter. The original plan and the results actually observed during the window did not line up. During the shift, it was initially handled as an observed discrepancy, not immediately classified as a confirmed defect in a particular filter implementation. A temporary recovery followed, but it happened before the cause was confirmed; this record preserves that sequence so the post-recovery state is not written up as though the root cause had already been found.

## Initial observations

Before the window began, the on-call staff determined the expected result from the original plan. Once the actual result was available, the first note recorded only that the two differed, without adding an explanation for the discrepancy. There was not enough information available to distinguish between a change in adapter values, a different execution order, or a step in the on-call procedure not being carried out as originally planned.

The initial investigation continued through the Doctrine entry point being used at the time. The failed command produced the first visible divergence, and its output was not overwritten by the later successful retry. This retention practice was later captured as a safeguard: "Keep failed reruns attached to the original record so successful retries don't overwrite the first divergence." Its only purpose was to preserve the context of the first failure, not to imply that the failure could already explain the entire chain.

## Shift timeline

- **Discrepancy identified**: The original plan and the observed result did not match. The on-call record first flagged the discrepancy without claiming that all Doctrine requests were affected.
- **Entry point revisited**: The investigation returned to `src/Doctrine/Orm/Filter/SearchFilter.php` and followed the call names in the notes from that time to examine behavior around the adapter layer. This location made it easy to return to the incident context.
- **Divergence observed**: The failed command did not produce the result expected under the original plan. At this point, it was still unclear whether the divergence occurred before the parameters entered the adapter layer or during subsequent execution.
- **Temporary recovery**: Results during the window returned to a state where observation could continue. The on-call staff did not discard the first failure record on that basis.
- **Postmortem write-up**: The discrepancy, recovery, and assessment of the cause were recorded separately. Recovery was an action that had taken place; the cause remained unresolved.

In the initial account at the time, `SearchFilter.php` could easily be read as "the problem has already been pinpointed here." This older assessment is still retained in the record: the file location was indeed the entry point used by the on-call staff to retrace the investigation, but it shows only that the investigation reached the Doctrine adapter layer, not that the file alone caused the discrepancy. When using this page again later, that older account should be read alongside the timeline; the cause must not be attributed based on the path alone.

## Impact and recovery

Known impact is limited to that on-call window: the original plan was not directly reflected in the results at the time, so the on-call staff interrupted their planned observation and took temporary action. The record provides no data on affected requests, resources, or callers beyond that scope, and there is no evidence that all Doctrine adapter behavior showed the same kind of discrepancy.

After the temporary recovery, the window could continue, but that shows only that the observed results had temporarily returned to a manageable state. It did not answer where the original plan and actual execution began to diverge, nor did it prove that the same conditions would not produce another divergence. The old record treated "no further discrepancy was observed after recovery" as a relatively strong signal; in retrospect, that was at most an observation from that shift, not a conclusion that the issue had been fixed for the long term.

Failed reruns remain under the first record because a successful retry can easily change how the incident is perceived: if only the successful result is retained, later readers will think the original discrepancy never occurred, or that the recovery action had already explained the failure. Keeping the failure context here is not meant to make too much of one anomaly, but to let later investigations still see the first divergence from the original plan.

## Open questions

Questions that still have no answers include: where the original plan first stopped being reflected in actual execution; whether the first divergence produced by the failed command was the earliest cause; and whether the temporary recovery bypassed the same conditions or merely changed the immediate result within the window. The existing record cannot connect these points into a single causal chain.

The fact that the on-call investigation reached the Doctrine entry point therefore remains useful: it can help locate the adapter context and call names reviewed at the time. It should no longer be treated as a root-cause conclusion. This page preserves a discrepancy within one window, the handling that kept the failure record from being overwritten, and the assessment that was still incomplete at the time of recovery; whether the implementation has since changed is outside the scope of this postmortem.

First return to the original entry point using the call name from FieldsBuilder, then place the failing command in the same replay window. This entry point is only the shared starting point for the two runs; it does not establish filter ownership, and processing further down the call chain has not been treated as already understood.

The log table keeps fixed settings and variables separate: the repository state, call entry point, and all other inputs stay unchanged, and only one input condition may vary. The second run did not replace both compatibility forms at once. If both forms were changed together, even a different result would not let us tell from this record which change the first divergence was related to.

Once the failing command appeared, the record stopped at the first visible divergence. The raw results were not subsequently classified as success or failure; a third run was not used to overwrite the first two runs, either. The review can confirm that the stopping point remains in its original location, but cannot confirm whether the divergence was caused by the input form, unexplored processing in the call chain, or the environment in which the command failed.

The earlier wording put too much weight on "single-variable," as though starting from the same repository state and changing only one input were enough to demonstrate a filter compatibility difference. That statement has been retained because it explains why the reruns were done that way at the time; it can now only be treated as an operational constraint. It allows observations near the entry point in the two runs to be placed side by side, but is not enough on its own to attribute the divergence.

What can be compared directly in these two run records, then, is a single input change under the same repository state and call entry point, along with the first difference exposed by the failing command. This does not establish that a particular compatibility form is supported or rejected. If both input forms need to be changed, keep a separate record to avoid folding different conditions into the same round of comparison.

For any further reruns, keep the repository state at graphql-runtime and the FieldsBuilder entry point fixed, and replace only one input condition from the existing log table. First retain the failing command and the first visible divergence; without new local observations, do not add a causal attribution to the earlier results.

In external updates, publish only the replay window, owner, and evidence entry point; do not make a premature call on behavior in the announcement. See DOC-51 for the decision and reservations on document export checks.

# Document Export Inspection Decision

The review of Starbridge Cloud Infrastructure Software's document export inspection was initially framed as a very broad question: whether checks should continue to start at the parameter-metadata entry point, or move to the adjustment window. Both framings could steer the discussion toward implementation placement across modules, and both could easily bring in schedules from peripheral projects. The scope that actually needs a decision is narrower: where this inspection round can start, and under what circumstances observations may be extended elsewhere.

The conclusion in the initial draft has not been withdrawn: retain the current entry point; the adjustment window remains an option held in reserve, but is not an approved change. The follow-up review added the assessment sequence and the boundaries of the record, rather than preassigning ownership to a particular module.

> This inspection round will not move the current parameter-metadata entry point for now. The review compared retaining the entry point with using the adjustment window, but the available material only supports continuing to use the former as the starting point for checks; the adjustment window is retained, not treated as a change approved in this round.

That passage was intended to distinguish two things. Retaining the entry point means the inspection still has a target it can start with; retaining the window means the review has not overlooked that direction. The two options are not equally mature, and "not yet adopted" must certainly not be written as "already proven unusable".

## Decisions Made

This round retains the current parameter-metadata entry point. It is the starting point for document export inspection, not the permanent home of the implementation or a judgment about placement across modules. Looking at `src/Metadata/ApiResource.php` and the related call names was only intended to match the parameter and metadata under discussion to the current target; this location cannot substitute for public calls and input comparisons.

The adjustment window is not approved to replace the entry point. The available material does not explain what results the adjustment window would produce, with the same input and a fixed version, that would justify a replacement. Simply moving the checks to a different point in time would give up a known starting point without gaining an alternative starting point that can be reviewed. The window is therefore retained in the decision so it can be revisited later with comparisons in hand, rather than serving as the default path for this round of work.

Peripheral projects will continue on their own schedules. The main task will refer to their status only when there is an actual dependency. Here, "actual dependency" does not mean excluding related projects, but not automatically treating work underway elsewhere as a prerequisite for the main task. If the inspection record directly equates relevance with dependency, it will then be difficult to tell whether an assessment of exports comes from the current checks or from impressions of schedules elsewhere.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[parameter-metadata Entry point] --> B[Actual public calls]
    B --> C[Comparisons using the same input]
    C --> D[Fixed version and visible results]
    D --> E[Implementation placement across modules]
    A --> F[Retain the current entry point]
    G[Adjustment window] --> H[Option held in reserve]
    I[Peripheral project schedules] --> J[Refer only when there is an actual dependency]
```

The arrows in the diagram indicate the order of discussion and where items belong in the record, not module call relationships. In particular, the arrow from the fixed version and visible results to implementation placement across modules means the latter can only enter the discussion once the preceding items have been fixed; it does not claim that a definite implementation location has already been established.

## Two Approaches Compared in the Review

The advantage of retaining the current entry point is not that it is closer to a predetermined answer, but that it can support the inspection method already agreed upon. Actual public calls can be examined from here; comparisons using the same input can be made from the same starting point; the version and visible results can also be fixed together. The resulting assessment is still limited, but those limits are clear: it only says where this inspection round begins, not where all adjacent modules should handle the problem.

This option also has a cost. Retaining the entry point does not automatically answer whether the adjustment window is more suitable, nor does it automatically settle implementation placement across modules. It defers both questions. The review accepted this cost because assigning a location in advance, before the input, version, and results are aligned, would leave the follow-up review without a common basis for comparison.

The appeal of the adjustment window is that it appears to bring the checks closer to another point in processing. But "closer" is not in itself a reason. Without a comparison using the same input, and without differences that remain identifiable after the version has been fixed, the window is merely a proposal to change the order of the narrative. It may be worth further investigation, but it is not yet enough to support a decision to replace the current entry point.

The objection, therefore, is not that "adjusting the timing is necessarily inappropriate". It is to presenting a window that has not yet been clearly explained as a change that has already happened when the prerequisite comparisons are missing. This distinction must be preserved: once the supporting material has been completed later, the window can be reviewed again; until then, the record can only retain its candidate status.

The two approaches are not permanently mutually exclusive roadmap options, either. This round allows checks to continue from the existing entry point while keeping questions about the adjustment window open. The difference is that the former has been approved as the starting point for work, while the latter has not yet become an inspection rule. Describing them as a long-term commitment to one or the other would go beyond the scope of this decision.

## Inspection Sequence

The sequence confirmed by the review is: first examine actual public calls, then compare using the same input, then fix the version and visible results, and only then discuss implementation placement across modules. This sequence is not a formality. If the public calls have not been confirmed, the discussion may already have started from the wrong entry point; if the inputs differ, differences in exports cannot establish whether the cause is an entry-point change or an input difference; if the version has not been fixed, the content observed before and after cannot be included in the same assessment.

"Fixing the version" does not mean the environment will never change again. It simply defines a comparable scope for the objects that a particular inspection depends on. Given the same input, the record must be able to identify which version the observed results belong to; otherwise, if the next check produces different exported content, there is no way to tell whether the window, the entry point, or the version itself caused the difference.

Likewise, "actual public calls" does not require completing a cross-module walkthrough first. It requires first confirming the calls the inspection actually encounters, then deciding whether it is worth expanding to adjacent locations. Working backward from the implementation location to the public entry point would dress up speculation as a premise for inspection; this reversal is precisely one of the reasons the adjustment window was not accepted in this round.

The cross-module issue has not been removed here. It remains on the list of questions, but is deferred until the entry point, input, and version can be distinguished. The resulting decision is limited in scope, but it avoids listing the implementation locations that different people remember side by side as conclusions of equal standing.

## Handling Peripheral Projects

The meeting materials require peripheral projects to proceed on their own schedules, with the main task referring only to status information for actual dependencies. This requirement directly affects how the document export inspection is written up. Peripheral projects may provide background and may later become actual dependencies; until a dependency has been confirmed, their progress should not fill the gaps in this round's discussion of the entry point or the window.

This approach does not require peripheral projects to stop, nor does it require the main task to wait until all adjacent work is complete. Both sides retain their own pace. The main task includes only dependencies that can already be confirmed in its current assessment, so that a change in a peripheral status does not, in turn, force the inspection conclusion to be interpreted as a scheduling conclusion.

Another easily confused distinction is between "relevance" and "dependency". Both the adjustment window and peripheral projects may be relevant to the cross-module discussion, but relevance only shows that something merits further examination; a dependency becomes part of the basis for the main task's assessment. This round has no material that elevates all related work to dependencies, so the record does not expand what it refers to.

DOC-01 contains limited-scope work records for the swagger-ui-bundle event exit, which can be read as adjacent material. This does not change the decision on this page: document export inspection still starts at the current entry point, the window is still not approved to replace the entry point, and peripheral status information still enters the main task only when there is an actual dependency.

## Follow-up Review Notes

The actual follow-up review did not provide new material sufficient to turn the adjustment window into an approved plan. It confirmed that checks should continue to start with actual public calls and comparisons using the same input, confirmed that the version and visible results must be fixed first, and also confirmed that implementation placement across modules should not be settled before these conditions are met.

The initial draft's judgment to "retain the entry point" therefore remains valid. What the follow-up review added was an explicit boundary: approve only the scope covered by the existing material. This boundary blocks two kinds of expansion at once. One is to describe work underway in peripheral projects as dependencies of the main task; the other is to describe the adjustment window under discussion as a completed replacement of the entry point. Both formulations skip the comparison sequence prescribed for this round.

Specific unresolved questions remain. Whether the adjustment window would change the interpretive scope of the current entry point has not yet been answered by results using the same input and a fixed version; nor has it been concluded whether those comparisons can settle implementation placement across modules. These questions are retained not to make the decision look open-ended, but to prevent later readers from mistakenly believing this round has already addressed them.

The next time the adjustment window is compared again, work should continue from the starting point left by this round: confirm the actual public calls, compare using the same input, fix the version and visible results, and then discuss placement. If any one of these is missing, the new comparison will still be insufficient to change the current decision.
